title: DAP Notes: Behavioral Health Example, Format, and Audit Rules
summary: See a behavioral health DAP notes example, why the Data section is the half that loses clinical evidence, and what payers read in the Assessment and Plan.
body_markdown:
DAP notes are the working format for a lot of behavioral health documentation, and the structure takes about a minute to learn: Data, Assessment, Plan. The part that costs clinicians time and costs clinics money is narrower than the format itself. It is what belongs in the Data section, and it is the reason a note that felt complete when you wrote it comes back flagged in a chart review.


Below is a full behavioral health DAP note example with a section by section breakdown, a quick reference table of what belongs where, a comparison against SOAP, BIRP and GIRP, the elements payers and auditors actually look for, the eight ways a DAP note fails a chart review, and what the format costs at a full caseload.


## What Is a DAP Note?


A DAP note is a session note with three sections. **Data** records what happened in the session, both what the client reported and what you observed. **Assessment** records your clinical interpretation of that data against the treatment plan and the diagnosis. **Plan** records what happens next: the intervention, any medication change, between-session work, the follow-up interval, and coordination with other providers.


DAP is widely used by counselors, clinical social workers and therapists, and it is a common house format in group programs and substance use treatment. Prescribers and psychiatric nurse practitioners more often work in SOAP. If your clinic runs both formats, that is worth knowing before you standardise on one.


Here is the whole format in one table.


Section What it records What a reviewer looks for


**D** for Data What the client reported in the session, and what you observed. Both halves, in that order. Symptom frequency and severity with numbers where numbers exist, plus mental status findings. Not a transcript.


**A** for Assessment Your clinical interpretation of that data against the diagnosis and the treatment plan. Diagnosis with specifiers and ICD-10 code, current severity, the numbered treatment plan goal being worked, and why this level of care continues.


**P** for Plan What happens next, and when. Named modality, medication changes with rationale, between-session tasks, a follow-up date or interval, coordination with other providers, risk review where indicated.


The abbreviation is read the same way in every setting that uses it. The D stands for Data, not Description and not Diagnosis, and that distinction is the one most often got wrong in supervision.

## A Behavioral Health DAP Note Example


Most published DAP examples are either generic or drawn from primary care. The one below is an individual therapy session with an adult client, written the way a note has to read to survive a payer review. Details are illustrative.


### Data


*Client attended a 53 minute individual session and arrived on time. Reports four panic episodes in the past week, down from seven the previous week, with the longest lasting close to ten minutes. Identifies freeway driving and an upcoming work presentation as the two consistent triggers. Completed the interoceptive exposure practice on four of seven days and describes the paced breathing as the only thing that interrupts the escalation. Sleep improved to six hours nightly from four. Observed alert and oriented, appearance appropriate, speech normal in rate and volume, mood reported as anxious with congruent and mildly constricted affect, thought process linear and goal directed, no perceptual disturbances, insight good, judgment intact. Denies suicidal and homicidal ideation on direct questioning.*


The documented length matters twice over. A session of 53 minutes or more is the floor for[90837 rather than 90834](https://www.mdhub.ai/blog-posts/90837-cpt-code) , so the number in your Data section carries a billing consequence as well as a clinical one.


Notice that the section carries two distinct kinds of evidence. The first half is the client's report, including numbers where numbers exist. The second half is your own observation, which in behavioral health means mental status findings rather than vitals. Both halves are load bearing.


#### What belongs in the Data section


- Presenting symptoms with frequency, severity and duration, using numbers wherever numbers exist
- Change since the last session, stated as a direction rather than a description
- Mood, sleep and appetite as reported by the client
- Adherence to between-session work, with the actual count rather than "good compliance"
- Events since the last session that bear on the treatment plan
- Observed appearance, behavior, speech rate and volume
- Affect, and whether it is congruent with the reported mood
- Thought process, thought content, insight and judgment
- A direct statement about suicidal and homicidal ideation, asked and answered
- Documented session length, because it sets the billable code


#### What a reviewer checks in the Data section


- That both halves are present: what was reported and what was observed
- That mental status findings appear, not vitals borrowed from a medical template
- That risk was asked about directly rather than assumed
- That the session length supports the code billed
- That the numbers in this section are the ones the Assessment then interprets


#### How the Data section fails


- It reads as a session summary in the client's voice with no independent observation
- It records "client reports feeling better" with no frequency, severity or duration
- It runs long as a narrative recap and buries the two or three findings that matter
- It repeats background history already documented in the intake
- It omits session length, which turns a coding question into an audit question


**Self-check:** read the Data section back and cross out every sentence that came from the client. If nothing clinical is left, the section is not finished.


### Assessment


*Panic disorder without agoraphobia (F41.0). Episode frequency has decreased for a second consecutive week, consistent with response to the interoceptive exposure protocol introduced in session four, and tracks treatment plan goal one, reducing panic episodes to two or fewer per week. Avoidance of freeway driving persists and remains the primary functional limitation. Partial adherence to between-session practice appears to reflect a shift-work scheduling barrier rather than motivational resistance. Continued weekly individual therapy is clinically indicated to consolidate exposure gains before session spacing is considered.*


The Assessment interprets, it does not restate. It names the diagnosis with its specifier and code, gives a direction of travel, ties the session to a numbered treatment plan goal, and says why the current level of care should continue. Those four moves are what a medical necessity reviewer is looking for.


#### What belongs in the Assessment section


- The diagnosis written out with its specifiers and its ICD-10 code
- Current severity, so the reviewer has something to weigh
- Direction of travel since the last session, tied to the data above
- The numbered treatment plan goal this session worked
- Response to the specific intervention being used, named
- Any barrier to progress, and whether it is clinical, practical or motivational
- Your reasoning for continuing, stepping up or stepping down the level of care


#### What a reviewer checks in the Assessment section


- That it interprets rather than restates the Data section
- That the diagnosis carries specifiers, not a bare code
- That a numbered treatment plan goal is named, which is what carries the Golden Thread
- That medical necessity for the current level of care is argued, not assumed


#### How the Assessment section fails


- It paraphrases the Data section back with no clinical judgment added
- It gives a diagnosis with no specifier, leaving the reviewer no severity to weigh
- It never names a treatment plan goal, so the note floats free of the plan
- It offers no reason why weekly frequency should continue


**Self-check:** if a reviewer could not tell from this section why the client still needs this service at this frequency, the Assessment has not done its job.


### Plan


*Continue weekly individual CBT. Advance the exposure hierarchy to a supervised ten minute freeway drive before the next session. Client to complete the daily panic log and interoceptive practice five of seven days. Introduce cognitive restructuring targeting catastrophic prediction in session ten. No medication change; client remains on a current prescription managed by the referring psychiatric nurse practitioner, and a coordination note will be sent this week. Next appointment 9 October at 10:00. Crisis plan reviewed and client confirmed access to the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline and the clinic after-hours line.*


Every element in that Plan is checkable by someone who was not in the room. That is the test. If a reviewer cannot tell what you are going to do, when, and why, the Plan has not done its job. For side by side comparison in the other direction, our[behavioral health SOAP note example](https://www.mdhub.ai/blog-posts/soap-note-example) works through the same standards in the four section format, and the[therapy note template guide](https://www.mdhub.ai/blog-posts/the-ultimate-therapy-note-template-guide-streamline-your-documentation-with-ai) covers the other formats a supervisor or payer may ask for.


#### What belongs in the Plan section


- The modality continuing or changing, named specifically
- The next step in the intervention, concrete enough to be checked
- Between-session tasks with a frequency target
- Any medication change with the rationale, or an explicit statement that there is none
- Coordination with other providers, and when it will happen
- A follow-up date or a stated interval
- Risk and crisis planning where clinically indicated, including what the client confirmed


#### What a reviewer checks in the Plan section


- That every element is checkable by someone who was not in the room
- That an interval or date is set rather than implied
- That the plan follows from the Assessment rather than repeating last session
- That crisis access is documented where risk was discussed


#### How the Plan section fails


- "Continue treatment" as the whole plan, which names no intervention and sets no interval
- No follow-up date, so the reviewer cannot see continuity of care
- Copy-forward from the previous note with nothing advanced
- Medication left unaddressed in a note where medication is clearly relevant


**Self-check:** hand the Plan to a covering clinician. If they cannot run the next session from it, it is not a plan.


## DAP vs SOAP Notes, and the Mistake in Between


The formats are closer than they look. DAP merges Subjective and Objective into Data and leaves the rest alone.


Element SOAP note DAP note


Sections Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan (four) Data, Assessment, Plan (three)


Where the client's own words go Subjective Data, first half


Where your clinical observation goes Objective Data, second half. This is the half that gets dropped.


Who tends to use it Psychiatric NPs, prescribers, medical settings, and payer-supplied templates Counselors, social workers, therapists, group and substance use programs


What a weak version looks like An Objective section filled with vitals instead of mental status findings A Data section that reads as a session summary with no observation


**Here is the mistake.** Because Data is a single field, it invites a single voice, and the voice that comes most naturally is the client's. So the section fills up with what was reported and quietly loses what was observed. The note still reads fluently. It has just stopped containing any independent clinical evidence.


That matters in two places. A supervisor reviewing the chart has no record that a mental status assessment happened. And a payer checking medical necessity sees a session that was attended and described but not clinically assessed, which is a weaker basis for approving the claim than the same session documented with observation included. The fix is mechanical: treat Data as two paragraphs, reported and observed, and never let the second one go missing.


### The two halves of a Data section


The fix for the most common DAP failure is mechanical. Write Data as two paragraphs and check that both are populated before you sign.


First half: what the client reported Second half: what you observed


Source The client, in session You, in session


Typical content Symptom frequency and severity, sleep, appetite, mood, adherence to between-session work, events since last session Appearance, behavior, speech, affect against reported mood, thought process and content, insight, judgment, risk


What makes it strong Numbers wherever numbers exist, and a direction of change Findings a second clinician could have made from the same room


What makes it weak A narrative recap of the conversation Vitals borrowed from a medical template, or nothing at all


Who reads it The reviewer checking that symptoms support the diagnosis The reviewer checking that the session was clinically assessed, not just attended


### DAP, SOAP, BIRP and GIRP side by side


Four formats cover almost all behavioral health documentation. They differ in how they slice the same clinical content.


Format Sections Who tends to use it Best suited to Most common failure


SOAP Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan Psychiatric NPs, prescribers, medical settings, payer-supplied templates Sessions where the medical and the psychiatric picture both matter An Objective section filled with vitals instead of mental status findings


DAP Data, Assessment, Plan Counselors, social workers, therapists, group and substance use programs Talk therapy where observation and report belong together A Data section that reads as a session summary with no observation


[BIRP](https://www.mdhub.ai/blog-posts/birp-notes) Behavior, Intervention, Response, Plan Community mental health, case management, substance use programs Sessions where what the clinician did needs to be visible on its own An Intervention section that names no specific technique


GIRP Goal, Intervention, Response, Plan Programs documenting explicitly against treatment plan goals Settings where every note must map to a numbered goal A Goal restated verbatim every session with no movement recorded


Progress note (unstructured) Free narrative Solo practices without a house format Almost nothing that faces a payer No consistent place for medical necessity, so reviewers have to hunt


The clinical content does not change between them. What changes is where each element lives, and therefore which element is easiest to lose. Our[behavioral health SOAP note example](https://www.mdhub.ai/blog-posts/soap-note-example) and[BIRP notes guide](https://www.mdhub.ai/blog-posts/birp-notes) work the same session through the other structures.


## What Payers and Auditors Read in a DAP Note


Reviewers do not grade prose. They look for specific elements and they look in specific places. In the Assessment: diagnosis with specifiers and ICD-10 code, current severity, the treatment plan goal being worked, and the reasoning for the level of care. In the Plan: modality, medication changes with rationale, between-session tasks, the follow-up date or interval, coordination with other providers, and a documented risk review where clinically indicated.


Two failure patterns are worth singling out. The first is a diagnosis without specifiers, which gives the reviewer no severity to weigh. The second is a Plan that says continue treatment, which names no intervention and sets no interval. Neither is a coding problem. Both are documentation problems, and both are cheaper to prevent inside the note than to appeal after a denial.


Element by element, this is what a reviewer is looking for and where they expect to find it.


Element Section What the reviewer wants to see What fails


Diagnosis Assessment Written out with specifiers plus the ICD-10 code A bare code, or a diagnosis with no specifier


Severity Assessment A current severity the reviewer can weigh Severity implied by tone rather than stated


Treatment plan link Assessment The numbered goal this session worked No reference to the plan at all


Medical necessity Assessment Reasoning for continuing at this level of care "Client is doing well" with no care-level argument


Symptom evidence Data Frequency, severity and duration, with numbers "Reports improvement" with nothing measurable


Clinical observation Data Mental status findings made by the clinician Only the client's own report


Risk Data Asked directly, answer recorded Risk not mentioned in a session where it is relevant


Session length Data Documented minutes that support the code billed No length recorded


Intervention Plan A named modality and a concrete next step "Continue treatment"


Follow-up Plan A date or a stated interval Nothing, or "as needed" by default


Coordination Plan Who will be contacted and when Referrals mentioned once and never closed


## The Eight Ways a DAP Note Fails a Chart Review


These are documentation failures rather than coding failures, which means every one of them is cheaper to prevent inside the note than to appeal after a denial.


- **The Data section has no observation.** Cause: one field invites one voice, and the client's voice comes first. Fix: write Data as two paragraphs, reported then observed, and never ship the note without the second.
- **The diagnosis carries no specifier.** Cause: the code is copied from the billing screen. Fix: write the diagnosis out in full in the Assessment, specifier included.
- **The Assessment restates rather than interprets.** Cause: it is written last, quickly. Fix: start the Assessment with a direction of travel, not a summary.
- **No treatment plan goal is named.** Cause: the goal number is in another document. Fix: name the numbered goal in every Assessment. This is the Golden Thread.
- **The Plan says "continue treatment".** Cause: nothing changed this week. Fix: state the next concrete step even when the modality is unchanged, and set the interval.
- **No session length is recorded.** Cause: the length lives in the scheduler, not the note. Fix: put the minutes in the Data section, because that is where a reviewer checks the code.
- **The note is copy-forward.** Cause: reconstruction from memory hours later, with the last note open. Fix: move the writing into the session.
- **Risk is absent from a session where it was relevant.** Cause: it was discussed and not recorded. Fix: a standing line in Data for ideation asked and answered, and crisis access in the Plan.


### A DAP progress note checklist to run before you sign


- Data contains both a reported paragraph and an observed paragraph
- Symptom frequency, severity and duration are stated with numbers where numbers exist
- Mental status findings are present, not vitals
- Ideation was asked about directly and the answer is recorded
- Session length in minutes is written down and supports the code billed
- Assessment names the diagnosis in full, with specifiers and ICD-10 code
- Assessment names the numbered treatment plan goal this session worked
- Assessment gives a reason why this level of care continues
- Plan names a modality and a concrete next step, not "continue treatment"
- Plan sets a follow-up date or interval, and records crisis access where risk was discussed


## The Golden Thread: Linking DAP Notes to the Treatment Plan


A single strong note is not the goal. What holds up in an audit is continuity across notes, the connection between a client's presenting problem, the treatment plan, and each session note that follows. That continuity is what clinicians call the Golden Thread, and the Assessment section is where a DAP note either carries it or drops it.


Carrying it by hand is the tedious part. It means remembering, in session eleven, which numbered goal you were working in session four and how the client has moved against it since. Do that across a full caseload and the thread frays in the DAP notes written last, which are also the notes written when you are most tired.


#### The four links the thread is made of


- The presenting problem recorded at intake
- A treatment plan goal, numbered, that addresses it
- An Assessment in each session note that names that goal and reports movement against it
- A Plan that advances the goal and sets the next review


Break any one of the four and an auditor reading the chart end to end sees a course of treatment with no stated destination.

## What DAP Notes Cost at Full Caseload


The format is not what consumes the time. Reconstruction is. A note written from memory two or three hours after the session takes longer, contains less, and is measurably weaker in the sections that protect the claim.


The pattern is not unique to behavioral health. Working across family medicine, internal medicine, cardiology and orthopaedics,[Sinsky and colleagues in Annals of Internal Medicine](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27595430/) found clinicians spent 27% of office time in direct clinical face time and close to half of it on records and desk work, plus further clerical hours after the day ended. That study did not cover behavioral health, so treat it as the shape of the problem rather than a number for your clinic. What behavioral health adds is a documentation load that is almost entirely narrative. Sustained, it feeds[clinician burnout](https://www.mdhub.ai/blog-posts/burnout-in-mental-health-professionals) , and the quieter cost arrives before anyone resigns: clinicians cap their own caseloads to keep the notes survivable, and a panel reads as full when it is really just administratively full. Our[behavioral health SOAP note example](https://www.mdhub.ai/blog-posts/soap-note-example) works through that arithmetic in detail.


The structural response is to move the writing into the session rather than after it. That is the premise behind[collaborative documentation](https://www.mdhub.ai/blog-posts/collaborative-documentation-mental-health) and behind AI documentation generally.


#### The arithmetic, worked through


Run your own numbers in place of these. The inputs below are illustrative, chosen to show the shape of the calculation rather than to describe any particular clinic.


- Sessions per week at a full outpatient caseload: **25**
- Minutes to write a focused DAP note immediately after the session: **5 to 10**
- Minutes to reconstruct the same note two or three hours later: **12 to 20**
- Weekly documentation time when notes are written immediately: **25 × 7.5 minutes = about 3.1 hours**
- Weekly documentation time when notes are reconstructed: **25 × 16 minutes = about 6.7 hours**
- Difference over a 46 week working year: **about 163 hours** , which is roughly four working weeks


The gap in that calculation is not the DAP format. It is the delay between the session and the note. Two figures from clinics running documentation inside the session rather than after it: clinicians using mdhub save **2+ hours per clinician per day** , and at Family Care Center clinicians save **between 6 and 20 minutes per note** .

What is the main difference between a DAP note and a SOAP note?


A SOAP note separates what the client reports (Subjective) from what the clinician observes (Objective). A DAP note merges those two into one Data section. The clinical content that has to be documented does not change. What changes is that DAP gives you a single container for two different kinds of evidence, which is why the observed half is the easier one to lose. If your Data section contains only what the client said, the note is missing the mental status findings a payer or supervisor looks for when checking that the session was clinically assessed rather than simply attended.


What is a DAP case note?


A DAP case note is a session note written in three sections: Data, Assessment and Plan. Data records what the client reported and what the clinician observed. Assessment records the clinician's interpretation of that data against the diagnosis and the treatment plan. Plan records what happens next, including the modality, between-session tasks, the follow-up interval and any coordination with other providers. The term case note is used interchangeably with progress note in most behavioral health settings, and the DAP structure is the same in both.


Can you provide an example of a DAP note?


Yes. A worked behavioral health example appears above: an individual therapy session with an adult client presenting with panic disorder, written the way a note has to read to survive a payer review. Data records four panic episodes in the past week, down from seven, with triggers, adherence, sleep, and a full mental status observation. Assessment names the diagnosis with its ICD-10 code, gives the direction of travel, ties the session to a numbered treatment plan goal, and argues why weekly care continues. Plan advances the exposure hierarchy, sets between-session work, records that there is no medication change, and gives a dated follow-up with a crisis plan review.


What belongs in the Data section of a DAP note?


Two things, deliberately. First, what the client reported: presenting symptoms, frequency and severity, mood, sleep, adherence to between-session work, and any events since the last session. Second, what you observed: appearance, behavior, speech, affect against reported mood, thought process and content, insight, judgment, and a direct statement about risk. Leave out narrative recaps of the whole conversation and background history you have already documented elsewhere. Data is evidence for the Assessment, not a transcript of the session.


What are the requirements for DAP notes?


There is no single national standard, so requirements come from the payer, the licensing board and the clinic's own policy. In practice reviewers look for the same elements every time. In Data: symptom frequency, severity and duration with numbers where numbers exist, mental status observation made by the clinician, a direct risk question asked and answered, and the documented session length. In Assessment: the diagnosis with specifiers and ICD-10 code, current severity, the numbered treatment plan goal being worked, and reasoning for the level of care. In Plan: a named modality, a concrete next step, between-session tasks, medication changes with rationale, coordination with other providers, and a follow-up date or interval.


What do payers require in a DAP note for it to hold up?


Payers read the Assessment and Plan to decide whether the service billed was medically necessary. The Assessment needs the diagnosis with its specifiers and ICD-10 code, the current severity, a link to the treatment plan goal being worked, and your reasoning for continuing or changing the level of care. The Plan needs the intervention or modality, any medication change with rationale, between-session tasks, the follow-up interval or scheduled date, coordination with other providers, and a risk or crisis review where clinically relevant. Entries such as "continue treatment" fail that review because they give the reviewer nothing to approve.


What does the D in a DAP note stand for?


Data. Not Description and not Diagnosis, which are the two most common misreadings in supervision. The distinction matters because Data is the evidence section, and it has to carry two kinds of evidence: what the client reported, and what the clinician independently observed. Reading the D as Description invites a session summary in the client's voice, which is exactly the failure that leaves a note with no clinical observation in it.


What does DAP stand for in mental health?


Data, Assessment, Plan. It is one of four note structures in common behavioral health use, alongside SOAP (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan), BIRP (Behavior, Intervention, Response, Plan) and GIRP (Goal, Intervention, Response, Plan). DAP is most common among counselors, clinical social workers and therapists, and it is a frequent house format in group programs and substance use treatment. Prescribers and psychiatric nurse practitioners more often work in SOAP.


Are DAP notes better than SOAP notes?


Neither format is clinically better. They slice the same content differently, and the right one is usually the one your clinic, supervisor or payer already expects. DAP is slightly faster to write because Data is one field rather than two. That speed is also its weakness: a single field invites a single voice, so the observed half is easier to lose than it is in SOAP, where Objective is its own labelled section. If your clinic runs both formats, standardise deliberately rather than by drift, and know that a weak SOAP note usually fails on vitals-instead-of-mental-status while a weak DAP note fails on missing observation.


How long should a DAP note take to write?


A focused behavioral health DAP note written immediately after the session is a five to ten minute task, and the merged Data section makes it slightly faster than the equivalent SOAP note. The number worth watching is not the first note of the day but the tenth. When notes are reconstructed hours later from memory, they get shorter and less specific exactly where specificity protects the claim. That is a workflow problem rather than a formatting problem, and it is the reason clinics move documentation into the session itself.
